summary: The Domain Name System (DNS) is an application layer protocol that translates human-readable domain names into computer-usable IP addresses using a distributed, hierarchical database. This hierarchy consists of root name servers, top-level domain (TLD) servers for extensions like .com, .org, and .in, and authoritative name servers holding actual domain records. Resolvers can interact with these servers using recursive queries, where the resolver does all the work, or iterative queries, where each server provides the address of the next server to contact. To improve efficiency, DNS caching stores recent answers based on a time to live (TTL) to reduce lookup time and network traffic. Finally, common DNS record types include A records for IPv4 addresses, AAAA records for IPv6 addresses, CNAME records for aliases, and MX records for mail servers.

key_terms.definition: DNS translates human-readable domain names, such as www.example.com, into IP addresses that computers use.
Root name servers sit at the top of the distributed, hierarchical DNS database.
Top-level domain (TLD) servers handle domains such as .com, .org and .in.
Authoritative name servers hold the actual records for a domain.
In a recursive query, the client asks the DNS resolver, and the resolver does all the work of contacting other servers and returns the final answer.
In an iterative query, each server replies with the address of the next server to ask, and the resolver contacts each one in turn.
DNS resolvers store recent answers for a time set by the TTL, which reduces lookup time and network traffic.
Common record types include an A record for IPv4, an AAAA record for IPv6, a CNAME record for an alias, and an MX record for a mail server.
